args.title: deviation-report.docx
args.body:
DEVIATION REPORT
Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement — Counterparty Markup Reconciliation
Data Privacy & Cybersecurity Practice Group

SCOPE AND SOURCES
This deviation report reconciles the counterparty's latest markup of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement against our original draft and firm playbook, incorporating the transfer impact summary and controlling partner instructions. This report addresses every deviation introduced by the counterparty and states the recommended disposition for each, grounded in the base materials in the matter file.

Source documents reviewed in full:
- Deal materials (matter file 9) — establishes the engagement, operative provisions, and firm-standard base position for the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement.
- Schedules and exhibits (matter file 87) — the disclosure schedules qualifying the base position: Schedule 3.7 (regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (survival matrix). Scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.
- Counterparty markup (matter file 35) — the counterparty's revision under review.
- Deal correspondence / partner instructions (matter file 113) — the controlling instruction for disposition priorities.
- Administrative correspondence (matter file 61) — misfiled distractor reflecting an unrelated engagement; expressly excluded and NOT relied upon.

DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP AND BASKET STRUCTURE
Counterparty change: The indemnification cap is silently reduced, and the indemnity basket is converted from a deductible to a tipping basket.
Base materials: Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the indemnification changes would silently shift, exposing the client to exposure that the original cap and deductible-basket structure were drafted to contain. Under the original playbook, the cap and a true deductible basket preserve full liability once the deductible threshold is crossed, whereas a tipping basket only exposes the excess above threshold.
Assessment: This is a material deviation that reallocates risk and, per Schedule 5.2, shifts retained liabilities onto the client.
Disposition: CONCEDE the basket conversion (from deductible to tipping basket), as expressly instructed by the partner in the controlling correspondence (matter file 113). The client accepts this concession. The indemnification cap reduction, however, is NOT conceded: the cap must remain at the firm-standard level because Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities make any further reduction a silent transfer of known exposure to the client. Counter any cap reduction to the original amount.

DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT DEFINITION (REGULATORY CARVE-OUTS)
Counterparty change: The definition of Material Adverse Effect (MAE) adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter.
Base materials: Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect directly with the added carve-outs. Carving out this regulatory action from the MAE definition would shield the counterparty from the precise regulatory circumstance that is already pending and disclosed, defeating the purpose of the MAE representation in the base draft.
Assessment: This deviation is factually significant because the pending inquiries are already known and scheduled; a carve-out tailored to them would hollow out the MAE protection.
Disposition: REJECT the MAE carve-outs. The carve-outs would neutralize the MAE provision in the one scenario that the transfer impact summary and Schedule 3.7 show is live and material. No partner instruction modifies this position. Require that the MAE definition remain as drafted in the original base, with the pending regulatory inquiries governed by the existing schedule disclosure rather than by an exclusion.

DEVIATION 3 — LIMITATION PERIOD / SURVIVAL REDUCTION
Counterparty change: A new limitation period shortens the survival of the core representations.
Base materials: Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change directly contradicts. Reducing survival of the core representations shortens the window in which a breach can be asserted, materially weakening the client's recourse.
Assessment: This is a direct contradiction of Exhibit B and is treated by the client as a fundamental, non-negotiable point.
Disposition: REJECT / WALK-AWAY ISSUE. Per the controlling partner instruction (matter file 113), the client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. This deviation must not be accepted under any circumstances; the survival periods in Exhibit B must be preserved as the firm-standard baseline. This is the highest-priority hard line in the negotiation.

CONTROLLING PARTNER INSTRUCTION
The deal correspondence (matter file 113) contains an email thread in which earlier messages stated a different priority ordering (e.g., treating the survival reduction as negotiable and the basket as a hard line). The LATEST message REVISES those priorities and controls: the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. Only the latest message governs this report. Accordingly:
- Basket conversion: concede (Deviation 1, partial).
- Survival reduction: non-negotiable walk-away issue (Deviation 3).
- Indemnification cap reduction and MAE carve-outs: reject, with no superseding instruction to the contrary.

MATERIAL EXCLUDED
The administrative correspondence (matter file 61) was misfiled into this matter's folder and concerns a different client engagement. It is excluded from all analysis and must not be relied upon.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDED POSITIONS
1. Basket conversion to tipping basket — ACCEPT (per controlling partner instruction).
2. Indemnification cap reduction — REJECT; hold at firm-standard cap per Schedule 5.2.
3. MAE regulatory carve-outs — REJECT; preserve MAE definition (Schedule 3.7 governs).
4. Survival reduction — REJECT / WALK-AWAY; preserve Exhibit B survival matrix (controlling partner instruction).
